demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
avoid anything that could be stressful
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette: Mateo was twenty-two when the afternoon turned to emergency. He had been helping a neighbor secure a rusted refrigerant line on an aging rooftop unit. When his wrench slipped, the heavy metal pipe gave way, and the sudden shift in weight threw the neighbor backward into a concrete vent. The crack of bone against masonry echoed in the sudden quiet before the shouting started. In the weeks that followed, Mateo’s world narrowed. He held onto a conviction that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, fixating on the split second his grip failed. When he could no longer trust his own body to respond correctly under pressure, he began to view his hands and instincts as an unrecognisable self, as if the person he had become was a stranger. This profound self-doubt made the traumatic memory itself feel detached, like footage shot for someone else. Whenever the past tried to surface, it forced its way into his mind uninvited, bringing with it the sharp, metallic tang of copper wire and the dusty, stagnant air of that rooftop. His profound self-doubt and unyielding guilt drove him to adopt rigid coping habits. He began to overanalyse every minor decision he made, going over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it. He actively avoided stressors, skipping complex service calls and turning down overtime. During the pause between HVAC diagnostic steps, an unbidden sensory intrusion immediately sparked a state of persistent threat. Whenever an ordinary quiet fell over a room, Mateo’s chest tightened, convinced that unusual silence meant something dangerous was about to happen. His heart would hammer against his ribs, a visceral physical reactivity that mirrored the panic he felt when the pipe fell. Yet, as his body braced for catastrophe, the very tension pulled the rooftop memory right back to the forefront of his awareness, sharpening the sensory recall and reinforcing the conviction that the moment of impact was still unfolding. These avoidance habits did not bring relief; they only cemented his distorted self-view. By isolating himself from work demands, he actively reinforced his belief that he was fundamentally broken, his original confidence buried under layers of hesitation. The more he dodged stressful situations, the more his environment narrowed until he only felt safe in a very limited number of places, almost entirely confined to the cab of his work truck where he could control the doors and windows. Even within this mobile sanctuary, the habit of avoidance directly intensified his physical reactivity to any sudden noise or tight space, the lingering threat response refusing to quiet. Approaching the one-year mark of the accident, Mateo found himself strictly avoiding anniversaries, tacking on extra shifts or taking cross-town routes to ensure he would never be in the vicinity of the date. He finally walked into the clinic when the isolation had become untenable; his crew noticed the frequent no-shows, and his friends stopped calling when he ghosted them entirely. He was terrified that he would never forgive himself for the injury he caused, but he desperately hoped to stop feeling like a ghost in his own life, to reclaim a body he trusted and a work he could navigate without constantly bracing for collapse.
